document.title: A Documentation System for Projects, Narrative, and Repeatable Work
document.headline: A Documentation System for Projects, Narrative, and Repeatable Work

workCoverage.coverageDescription: Covers approximately six to seven hours of August 1, 2026 design work that transformed an implicit documentation habit into a project-aware framework. The work produced a draft document-sidecar template, a procedural summary.md template, and a twenty-step documentation workflow, while defining project records, narrative authority, project-delta reconciliation, supervisor reading paths, staged instructions, validation, publication, communication, and bootstrap limitations.

subject.mainFocus: Designing a project-aware, narrative-preserving, stateful documentation framework with separate project records, summary instructions, document sidecars, workflow specifications, supervisor reading paths, publication artifacts, and explicit authority boundaries.
subject.description: A project-aware documentation framework for preserving work narrative, project context, workflow state, structured records, publication artifacts, and supervisor-readable updates.

narrative.promptingSituation: Klinswork had accumulated substantial work across conversations, HTML updates, sidecars, screenshots, applications, repositories, catalogs, and memory, but lacked an authoritative project layer explaining what each enduring undertaking was, how it related to others, its current state, and how each new body of work changed that state.
narrative.initialUnderstanding: The immediate problem appeared to be an underspecified document-sidecar template. Review showed that the missing responsibilities could not responsibly be solved by enlarging one descriptive JSON record.
narrative.intendedOutcome: Create a coordinated documentation architecture that preserves project identity, work narrative, evidence, state changes, audience-specific views, repeatable workflow, publication materials, and durable handoffs.
narrative.approach: Distinguish document records from project records, identify summary.md as the narrative authority, constrain the sidecar to describing HTML, create a procedural summary instruction set, reconstruct the full documentation process as a twenty-step workflow, and define focused instructions at stage boundaries.

progression.title: Separated projects from documents
progression.description: Recognized that dated work updates and enduring projects require different records and authority.
progression.result: A future project-record layer became the next major structural requirement.

progression.title: Identified the authoritative narrative source
progression.description: Rejected finished HTML as the preferred future source for project understanding and selected approved summary.md instead.
progression.result: HTML, sidecar, email, image brief, and project delta can derive from one narrative source.

progression.title: Preserved causal narrative and multiple audiences
progression.description: Required prompting situation, changing understanding, failures, turning points, method, and supervisor callouts.
progression.result: Technical depth and supervisor skimming can coexist in one document.

progression.title: Separated descriptive and procedural artifacts
progression.description: Constrained the sidecar to document description and made the summary template an instruction set.
progression.result: Each artifact gained a clearer authority boundary.

progression.title: Formalized the entire workflow
progression.description: Encoded nine phases and twenty steps with state, inputs, outputs, validation, review, automation, and next-step rules.
progression.result: The collaboration can operate as a staged, stateful pipeline.

problemsEncountered.problem: The sidecar risked absorbing project records, workflow instructions, summary narrative, publication state, and roadmap authority.
problemsEncountered.effect: One file would become oversized in purpose and duplicate several distinct systems.
problemsEncountered.resolution: Restricted sidecar authority to describing the finished HTML and its represented project contribution.

problemsEncountered.problem: Future project context might be reconstructed from finished HTML.
problemsEncountered.effect: Downstream presentation compression could become mistaken for authoritative project understanding.
problemsEncountered.resolution: Defined project records and approved summary.md as future source context, using HTML reconstruction only for legacy bootstrap work.

problemsEncountered.problem: A list of accomplishments would flatten the method and changing understanding.
problemsEncountered.effect: Future readers could recover results but not reasoning, failed paths, or reusable lessons.
problemsEncountered.resolution: Made chronological and causal narrative mandatory in the summary and structured in the sidecar.

problemsEncountered.problem: A separate supervisor-only document could drift from the technical record.
problemsEncountered.effect: The same work would require parallel rewriting and could become inconsistent.
problemsEncountered.resolution: Embedded ordered supervisor callouts and jump navigation inside the complete HTML.

problemsEncountered.problem: Loading every project and instruction for every operation would recreate context overload.
problemsEncountered.effect: The system would become slow, confusing, and difficult to maintain.
problemsEncountered.resolution: Load durable project context plus one focused instruction set at each workflow boundary.

narrative.methodEstablished: At each workflow boundary, load the authoritative project context, the approved output from the preceding stage, and one focused instruction set; perform the transformation; validate it; record the resulting state; and hand off to the next stage.
narrative.result: Three coordinated JSON artifacts and a documented twenty-step workflow now provide the first working structure of a project-aware documentation system.
lessonsLearned: Project records and document records answer different questions.
Narrative authority should be captured before downstream publication formatting.
Descriptive schemas and procedural instruction sets should remain separate.
One complete document can support multiple reader paths.
A generated catalog should not replace its individual source records.
Explicit bootstrap uncertainty is more trustworthy than invented completeness.

callouts.title: What was built
callouts.text: Three coordinated JSON artifacts now define the first working structure of a project-aware documentation system: a richer document sidecar, an instruction set for creating durable narrative summaries, and a twenty-step documentation workflow.

callouts.title: Why this matters
callouts.text: The framework reduces repeated reconstruction. Future work can load the right project context and the focused instruction set for the current workflow stage instead of requiring every conversation to carry the entire system at once.

callouts.title: Current status
callouts.text: The three JSON files were created and validated structurally. They are usable as drafts, but the system has not yet completed an end-to-end publication cycle, and formal project records do not yet exist.

callouts.title: What remains
callouts.text: The next layer is the project-record system itself. After that, the templates must be tested through real documentation cycles, the supervisor callouts implemented in the standard HTML template, and validation and indexing automation added.

callouts.title: Next operational step
callouts.text: Create project files that define each major undertaking, its purpose, scope, relationships, current state, and roadmap. No outside action is required during this bootstrap stage.

general.summary: The August 1 bootstrap work created the first coordinated structure for project-aware Klinswork documentation: a richer sidecar, a procedural narrative-summary template, and a twenty-step workflow.

technical.summary: The framework separates project authority, narrative authority, HTML presentation, sidecar description, project-state delta, catalog aggregation, and workflow procedure. It uses staged context loading and focused instruction sets at workflow boundaries.

projectSpecificLessons: The Klinswork documentation catalog cannot substitute for authoritative project records.
The approved Markdown summary should bridge active work, publication, and project-state reconciliation.
Legacy HTML reconstruction is acceptable only as a documented bootstrap exception.
generalLessons: Document identity and project identity require separate records.

sections.title: Executive Summary
sections.contentSummary: What changed This body of work addressed a persistent problem in the way Klinswork projects have been developed and documented: substantial work has been completed and described in many individual conversations, work updates, HTML pages, sidecars, screenshots, applications, repositories, and memories, but there has not yet been a stable project layer explaining what each enduring undertaking is, how it relates to the others, where it currently stands, or how a new body of work changes its state. The immediate work began with a review of the existing document-sidecar model. That model was useful for describing individual HTML work-update documents, but it was not designed to represent project identity, project history, the narrative of how work unfolded, roadmap reconciliation, audience-specific relevance, reusable knowledge, or the complete documentation workflow. sections.title: Situation Before the Work
sections.contentSummary: The problem The existing documentation system was extensive but document-centered. Individual work updates could describe what happened during a specific period, and the cumulative catalog could make those documents searchable. However, the catalog did not provide a durable model of the projects producing those updates. This created several practical problems: A project had to be reconstructed from scattered documents. A new conversation could learn what happened but not always what enduring undertaking the work belonged to. The current project state and roadmap were not stored authoritatively. The reasoning and method behind a result could disappear into a simplified list of accomplishments. Technical details and supervisor-relevant information were mixed together. The documentation workflow itself had to be repeatedly reconstructed. A brief new prompt could not reliably be placed into a larger project and workflow context. sections.title: Narrative of the Work
sections.contentSummary: How the method emerged The first problem: identifying projects from documents The work began by examining an existing cumulative work-update catalog and its metadata. The catalog contained several dated updates relating to Inventory, Work Queue, Calendar, shared locations, and the documentation system itself. From that review, a distinction emerged: A work-update record describes a dated document. A project record describes an enduring undertaking. The existing catalog could show which apps and topics appeared in an update, but it could not reliably answer what the project was, what its durable goal was, how it related to other projects, what state it was in before the update, or what remained afterward. This led to the first major architectural decision: add a project layer above document records rather than trying to infer project identity repeatedly from HTML updates. The second problem: identifying the authoritative source An early possibility was to derive project context by rereading the finished HTML work update. That approach…

sections.title: Knowledge Produced
sections.contentSummary: Reusable understanding Project-Specific Lessons A document catalog cannot substitute for project definitions. Project state must be reconciled at documentation time, not reconstructed only when work resumes. A durable summary must preserve both narrative and technical accounting. Audience-specific presentation can be layered onto one complete source document. A sidecar is most useful when its authority is clearly bounded. General Lessons Structured collaboration improves when state, context, procedure, and evidence are stored separately. Instruction sets are more useful when they describe where they operate within a larger workflow. A model does not need all information at all times; it needs the correct context at the transition between stages. Historical accuracy requires preserving failed approaches and uncertainty, not only successful outcomes. Automation becomes safer when every stage has explicit inputs, outputs, validation, and handoff conditions. Recurring Problems Reconstructing project identity from scattered outputs.…
